assumptions: The app targets modern web browsers (PWA) as the primary platform to maximize team accessibility and ease of adoption.
A centralized sync server is acceptable to coordinate synchronization, store persistent backups, and manage user identity.
Users require a rich text editing interface (e.g. lists, headings, formatting) rather than plain text or markdown.
Media files (images/attachments) are secondary to text synchronization and can be handled via lazy uploading/downloading once online.
candidates: Yjs + TipTap/ProseMirror (CRDT-based rich text editor with real-time and offline collaborative sync)
Automerge + custom document editor (JSON-based document CRDT)
Electric SQL / RxDB / Replicache (Local-first relational/document database synchronization engines)
Git-like branching and manual merge reconciliation for notes/sections
confirmed: Local-first architecture: The application must store and manage data locally by default.
Offline editing: Team members must be able to create, view, and edit notes without an active internet connection.
Automatic merge on reconnect: Notes must sync and merge automatically once a network connection is recovered.
Overwrite prevention: The system must prevent team members' edits from easily overwriting each other when merging.
conflicts: Offline Collaboration vs Identity/Permissions: Collaborative editing requires knowing who edited what to enforce permissions, but offline-first means authorization status cannot be validated against a server in real-time.

Automatic Character-Level Merging vs User Intent: While CRDTs automatically merge changes to avoid manual conflicts, overlapping edits can still lead to semantic gibberish or logical conflicts (e.g., duplicated action items) that technically 'overwrite' or disrupt a user's intent.

gaps.dependency: CRDT vs Database Sync Engine selection
gaps.impact: Directly determines the feasibility of the 'cannot easily overwrite others' changes' requirement.
gaps.reason: CRDTs (Yjs) allow real-time character-level merging, whereas local-first DB sync (Replicache/RxDB) works at the document/row level. This choice dictates the entire tech stack.

gaps.dependency: Platform-specific storage and file system APIs
gaps.impact: Affects storage persistence guarantees (IndexedDB can be cleared by browsers, native SQLite/OPFS is more persistent).
gaps.reason: We need to know whether to build a Web App (PWA) or a Desktop App (Tauri) for local-first storage persistence.

gaps.impact: Affects permission checks and edit history tracking when offline.
gaps.reason: If a user is offline, they cannot authenticate with a remote OAuth provider. We need a way to sign in / identify users offline.

options.impact: Uses IndexedDB/OPFS for storage. Easy to share links, works on all devices offline, but browser storage is subject to eviction.
options.label: Web App (PWA)

options.impact: Allows native SQLite databases, robust filesystem access, and guaranteed storage persistence, but requires manual installation.
options.label: Desktop App (Tauri / Electron)

options.impact: Convenient for on-the-go meetings, uses SQLite, but editing long notes on mobile can be cumbersome.
options.label: Mobile-first (React Native / Flutter)

questions.question: What platform should be the primary target for this local-first meeting notes application?
questions.reason: Determines the storage engine, offline capabilities, and deployment complexity.
questions.recommendation_reason: PWA offers low friction for team collaboration, offline capabilities via Service Workers, and cross-platform compatibility without native installation.

options.impact: No manual conflict prompts; changes merge gracefully, but might require minor manual cleanup if edits overlap semantically.
options.label: Automated character-level merge (CRDT / Yjs)

options.impact: Users explicitly review and choose which version of a paragraph/section to keep. Very safe but high friction.
options.label: Block-level versioning & manual review (Git-like)

options.impact: Simpler to implement, but edits from one of the users are discarded entirely if they edit the same document.
options.label: Document-level branching with Last-Write-Wins (LWW)

questions.question: How should conflicts be resolved when multiple offline edits are merged?
questions.reason: Crucial for the core requirement of 'not easily overwriting others' changes'.
questions.recommendation_reason: Yjs merges character-level changes automatically in a conflict-free manner, providing a Google Docs-like experience even after offline editing.

options.impact: Requires server hosting, but provides a reliable source of truth, secure backups, and easy team permissions.
options.label: Centralized Sync Server

options.impact: No server hosting costs, high privacy, but requires devices to be online on the same local network simultaneously to sync.
options.label: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Local Sync (e.g., WebRTC)

questions.question: How should synchronization work when the network is restored?
questions.reason: Decides the infrastructure architecture and backend requirements.
questions.recommendation: (Recommended) Centralized Sync Server (e.g., Yjs websocket server or Electric SQL)
questions.recommendation_reason: A centralized server makes user identity verification, persistence, sharing links, and initial sync setup extremely reliable.

risks: High architectural complexity of CRDTs/OT compared to standard REST-based client-server apps.
Browser storage limits (IndexedDB/OPFS limits) if notes contain large attachments or history.
Semantic merge conflicts: CRDTs merge text safely at the character level, but can produce unreadable sentences if users edit the same line.
First-time load and seed sync performance as notes database grows.
unknowns: Target deployment platforms (Web, Desktop, or Mobile) and local storage size requirements.
Identity model and user authentication flow when offline.
P2P local network sync requirement vs centralized server-facilitated sync.
Granularity of conflict resolution (character-level real-time vs block-level vs document-level).
